    Northern lights could be visible from 19 U.S. states this week due to a moderate to strong geomagnetic storm, making them brighter and pushing them farther south than usual. Best viewing window is late Wednesday night, March 18, into early Thursday morning, March 19, typically between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. local time. States with the best chances include Alaska, much of the northern U.S. (Idaho, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Oregon, South Dakota, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, Wyoming) plus northern parts of Indiana, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. For best views, go to a dark location away from city lights, find a clear north-facing horizon, and use aurora forecast tools or apps to track real-time conditions. #northernlights #usa #alaska #melodymocktail

    NRI community resource platform
    There are decent chances for some geomagnetic storming this weekend and auroral displays further equatorward than usual. NOAA SWPC has a G2 / moderate storm watch for Thursday March 19 and a G1 / minot storm watch for Friday March 20. This is in response to at least FOUR CMEs currently on the way to Earth. The main CME was launched after an M2.7 flare from AR 4392 on March 16 (peaking at 1215 UT). This had a very impressive EUV blastwave, but the coronagraph signatures were not that apparent. That CME was initially modeled by NASA M2M to impact Earth at 12 UT on March 19 and NOAA SWPC had the initial impact around 9 UT on March 19. SWPC has refined their model earlier now to 3 UT on March 19 which is around 10 pm CDT on Wednesday. Other agencies including the UK Met Office and models such as HUXt have this CME arriving much later, potentially as late as early on March 20 or Thursday night. Besides the M2.7 CME, there are at least three other smaller eruptions currently listed by NA

    Effects. What are the effects of a geomagnetic storm?

    Duration. How long do geomagnetic storms last?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    Geomagnetic storms vary greatly in length, from intense peaks lasting hours (even just 6 hours) to main activity that can last 12 to 48 hours, with overall impacts potentially extending for days or weeks, especially during powerful events driven by solar flares or Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs). Shorter, intense bursts can be followed by prolonged periods of moderate disturbances from High-Speed Streams (HSS) from coronal holes, often lasting 3-4 days. 
    Typical Durations:
    • Short Storms/Peaks:
      A severe storm might have a peak intensity for around 6 hours, while the overall event could be shorter, notes the European Space Agency (ESA). 
    • Moderate Storms:
      The main phase, when the geomagnetic field is most disturbed, often lasts for 12 to 48 hours. 
    • Longer Events:
      High-speed solar wind streams can cause geomagnetic activity and auroras for 3 to 4 days. 
    • Extreme Events:
      The legendary Carrington Event in 1859 showed sustained impacts, with disturbances lasting days, notes Wikipedia. 
    Factors Influencing Duration:
    • Cause:
      CMEs often create intense, shorter storms, while coronal holes produce long-duration, but sometimes less severe, storms. 
    • Solar Cycle:
      Storms are more frequent and can be stronger during solar maximum (the peak of the 11-year solar cycle). 
    • Solar Wind:
      The speed and density of solar wind particles hitting Earth, and the orientation of the solar wind's magnetic field, dictate storm intensity and length.

      Is a geomagnetic storm the same as the northern lights?
